newsitem.title: USA: US Stockpile plans extra vanadium, columbium sales.
newsitem.headline: US Stockpile plans extra vanadium, columbium sales.

text.p: The U.S. Stockpile expects to sell an additional 198 short tons of vanadium in the current fiscal year which would deplete the government's surplus hoard of the metal, Stockpile administrator Richard Connelly said.

The stockpile has already sold the 200 short tons of vanadium it was allocated in the current fiscal year, beginning October 1, 1996, and has asked Congress for permission to bring forward the sales allocation it had for the next fiscal year, which begins October 1.
Connelly, speaking at Ryan's Notes vanadium, molybdenum and columbium conference, said it would be July at the earliest when the extra vanadium would be up for sale.
"I think we will get the authority, and that will exhaust our inventory," Connelly said.
The vanadium has been sold on a sealed bid basis and he expected this to continue with the new allocation, with monthly offers in July, August and September or until exhaustion.
The Stockpile is also looking for extra ferro-columbium (known outside the U.S. as ferro-niobium) to sell in the current fiscal year.

The fiscal year 1997 allocation is 60,000 pounds of contained columbium in ferro-columbium and 31,288 pounds of this was sold on March 21. Total Stockpile inventory is 930,911 pounds of contained metal in ferro-columbium.

Connelly said the Stockpile has initiated proceedings in Congress to get permission to sell a maximum of 200,000 pounds of columbium in 1997 fiscal year which ends September 30, on a negotited bid basis.
"We expect to get the authority in July," Connelly said.

Meanwhile the Stockpile is also seeking industry comment on a proposal to sell some of its 34,000 tons of titanium sponge stock, most likely in the fiscal year beginning October 1 at the earliest, Connelly said.

Connelly also reiterated that Stockpile fully expected to go ahead with its cobalt sealed bid sale for 1 million pounds on April 7, an offer postponed from March 31 following an application for a temporary restraining order against the sale by Minor Metals Inc trading company.
The case was scheduled to be heard on Thursday afternoon in the U.S Federal Claims Court, but Connelly did not expect an outcome immediately.

Some delegates at the conference wished that more information about the outcome of negotiated sales would be made public, possibly a few months after they were concluded in order to assess market impact. Connelly said this was something that may be considered.
